answer:
Hypothesis (data-grounded, within-sample interpretation)

"Across the NLSY79 respondents in this dataset, the median family net wealth of white individuals (proxied by the NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC cohort) was consistently higher than that of Black and Hispanic individuals in every wealth wave from 1985 onwards, and the gap widened over time. In 1985 the white-proxy median was $3,500, compared with $1,600 for Black and $500 for Hispanic individuals — i.e., 2.2× and 7.0× the Black and Hispanic medians, respectively. In 1990 the medians were $12,972 (white-proxy), $4,800 (Black), and $1,600 (Hispanic), i.e., 2.7× and 8.1×. By 1996 the medians were $42,600 (white-proxy), $9,800 (Black), and $2,562.5 (Hispanic), i.e., 4.3× and 16.6×, so Black and Hispanic median wealth had fallen to about 23% and 6% of the white-proxy median. The absolute White–Black gap grew from about $1,900 (1985) to $8,200 (1990) to $32,800 (1996), and the White–Hispanic gap grew from about $3,000 to $11,400 to $40,000. Because the white-proxy median grew roughly 12× from 1985 to 1996 while Black and Hispanic medians grew only about 6× and 5×, both the absolute gap and the ratio widened monotonically across 1985→1990→1996 — the median wealth advantage of white individuals over Black and Hispanic individuals was persistent and increasing from 1985 onwards."

Supporting computed numbers actually used (per-year complete cases, unweighted, medians of family net wealth in USD; all Mann–Whitney tests White-proxy vs each group p<0.001):

| Year | White(proxy) | Black | Hispanic | W−B | W/B | W−H | W/H |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | 3,500 | 1,600 | 500 | +1,900 | 2.19× | +3,000 | 7.00× |
| 1990 | 12,972 | 4,800 | 1,600 | +8,172 | 2.70× | +11,372 | 8.11× |
| 1996 | 42,600 | 9,800 | 2,562.5 | +32,800 | 4.35× | +40,038 | 16.62× |

Within-group median growth 1985→1996: White(proxy) 3,500→12,972→42,600 (12.2×); Black 1,600→4,800→9,800 (6.1×); Hispanic 500→1,600→2,562.5 (5.1×). Bootstrap 95% CIs for the medians do not overlap between groups in any year (e.g., 1996 White 40,750–46,000; Black 8,198–11,550; Hispanic 2,000–3,000).

Key caveats framing this as a within-sample interpretation (not nationally representative totals): (1) "white" is proxied by the NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC cohort label, the closest available category; (2) "from 1985 onwards" = the three available net-wealth waves (1985, 1990, 1996); (3) wealth is family-level, assigned to each individual respondent (one row per person); (4) estimates are unweighted (no survey-weight column in the file; NLSY79 oversampled Black/Hispanic youth); (5) missingness rises over time and is group-imbalanced, most notably in 1996 where 52.6% of NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC respondents lack a wealth value (vs 31.7% Black, 33.4% Hispanic), so later waves describe observed respondents; (6) net wealth includes negative and zero values (retained) and is top-coded at the same ceiling per year across all three groups, which does not affect medians.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 rows, unique respondent IDs). Mapped 'Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979' to groups (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC, 3=WHITE-PROXY NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC). For each of the three net-wealth waves (1985, 1990, 1996) computed per-group medians on per-year complete cases (negative/zero wealth retained), plus 2,000-draw bootstrap 95% CIs, means, quartiles, and neg/zero/pos shares. Computed absolute (White−Black, White−Hispanic) and ratio (White/Black, White/Hispanic) median gaps per year, within-group median growth across waves, and Mann–Whitney U tests for White vs Black and White vs Hispanic per year. Unweighted (no survey-weight column exists in the file). Final hypothesis is framed as a within-sample comparison with caveats on the white proxy, family-level wealth assignment, rising/imbalanced missingness, top-coding, and absent survey weights.
